newsitem.title: USA: U.S. set to join Bosnia "stabilization force".
newsitem.headline: U.S. set to join Bosnia "stabilization force".

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Friday the United States has agreed in principle to send 8,500 U.S. troops to Bosnia next year within a new 31,000-man peacekeeping force expected to remain until June 1998.

Clinton defended the extension of a U.S. military presence in Bosnia beyond this year, as once promised, as necessary to assure continued peace in the former Yugoslav province. He denied he intentionally delayed announcing the controversial decision until after he was re-elected last week.
The Pentagon said the new force under NATO control would total 31,000 and would replace the current 50,000-strong peace implementation force known as IFOR. There are 15,000 U.S. troops in that force.

"The (IFOR) operation was a success, but the patient is still in danger of dying," Defence Secretary William Perry told reporters of the need for what he called the new "stabilization force" in Bosnia.

In separate news conferences, Clinton and Perry said the current force had done its job well but more time was needed for reconstruction and political reconciliation in Bosnia, battered by years of brutal factional fighting.

"I have decided to instruct the United States representative to NATO to inform our allies that in principle the United States will take part in a follow-on force in Bosnia," Clinton said at the White House.
"We believe the size will be about 8,500," he said of the planned U.S. participation, adding: "There will be an American commander and tough rules of engagement."

He said the total would be reviewed every six months and cut in half by the end of 1997. He added, "We will propose to our NATO allies that by June of 1998, the mission's work should be done and the forces should be able to withdraw."

"For my agreement in principle to become a commitment, I must be satisfied that the final recommendationm NATO adopts and the operational plan it develops are clear, limited and achieveable," he said.

Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said the plan was to cut the new force to about 13,500, about 5,000 of them Americans, by the autumn of next year and to have all troops out by June of 1998.
The decision by the Democratic president to send the troops to a new force was expected to win grudging approval from the newly elected Republican-controlled Congress.

Dan Coats, Republican senator from Indiana and a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Clinton's action on Bosnia reflected the "seat-of-the-pants reactive foreign policy that's been the plague of this administration"
But he told a press conference the move would finally be supported by Congress.
When he sent the U.S. troops to Bosnia nearly a year ago, Clinton promised they would be out by the end of this year.

"Today, the Bosnian people are far better off than they were a year ago. Their prospects for peace and freedom are much brighter," he said. "Bosnia's bitter harvest of hatred, however, has not disappeared."

Most of the 16 NATO nations have informally approved the new force and Russia and other non-NATO states would continue to take part in the follow-on effort, which would also station about 3,000 German troops in Bosnia.

Although, the United States has begun to withdraw its 15,000 troops in IFOR, it is currently sending in about 7,500 troops to help protect that withdrawal. Much of that cover force is already scheduled to remain until March and apparently would now become the vanguard of the the new force.

Representatives to the North Atlantic Council, NATO's political arm, will meet in Brussels on Monday and are expected to opt for the continuing peacekeeping force over other alternatives, according to NATO officials.

U.S. Army Gen. George Joulwan, NATO's military commander, will then seek specific commitments of troops from NATO and other countries to draw up a final plan, which would be given formal approval at separate meetings of NATO foreign and defence ministers in Brussels in mid-December.
